FIGURE 6: POLITICAL-MILITARY RELATIONSHIPS In the final analysis Rome just refused to give up when a less robust nation would surely have succumbed. Carthage and Hannibal did not adequately appreciate the recent lesson of the 1 st Punic War. In the 1 st Punic War, a mainly naval war, Rome repeatedly lost its fleet, either in action or to storms. Over 100,000 men and thousands of ships were lost. Each time the Romans rebuilt the fleet and regained control of the seas from the historically superior maritime power - Carthage 85 

23 3. ATTACK THE ENEMY'S STRATEGIC CENTER OF GRAVITY The Roman strategic center of gravity was the political will of the Roman Senate. Carthaginian strategy however was aimed at separating Roman allies. Once allies were separated, such as in Southern Italy, Hannibal proved incapable of providing the garrisons needed to defend them when his army was not in their immediate vicinity. Carthage's best opportunities for attacking the will of the Roman Senate were following Hannibal's decisive victories at Lake Trasimene and Cannae. No Roman army stood between Hannibal and Rome in both cases. One of his lightening advances on Rome might have broken the will of the Senate. 86 Instead he chose to concentrate on southern Italy and consolidate his newly acquired allies. Hannibal probably could not have taken Rome by storm as he lacked a siege train. Hannibal had taken eight months to reduce the minor city of Saguntum, his only successful siege operation. However, a march on Rome following Cannae might have forced the Romans to a negotiated peace with Rome in a position of weakness. Hannibal's only march on Rome occurred from a position of weakness. It was a desperate attempt to relieve the Roman siege of the key city of Capua and it failed miserably when the Romans recognized it as such. 87 

The Romans very clearly went after the Carthaginian strategic center of gravity - the political will of the Carthaginian oligarchy. Their strategy aimed at both the home city of Carthage and the financial heart of the very commercial Carthage - Iberia. Forced to fight for its survival in Italy, Rome was still able to maintain pressure on Carthage through operations in Iberia. Once Iberia was secured Rome moved directly against the North African homeland of Carthage. Scipio's presence outside the walls of Carthage forced the oligarchy to recall Hannibal to North Africa. Hannibal's defeat at Zama broke the political will of the Carthaginians. 4. STRATEGIC ASSUMPTIONS Strategic assumptions must be valid or a plan is doomed to failure. Carthage assumed Rome's Italian and Latin allies would defect following Roman battle losses. This would rob Rome of its significant manpower advantage and Hannibal could then dictate terms to a defeated Rome. Hannibal had a relatively contemporary lesson that should have provided him an insight into the validity of this assumption. Pyrrhus also tried to influence Italian tribes to leave their alliance with Rome. Rome was defeated several times in battle but remained resilient and the allies remained loyal. Rome refused to yield while the Epiran army was being destroyed in a series of bloody battles. This took place at a time when Rome's allies were even less tied to Rome, where such a strategy would have had a greater chance of success. 24 Romans forced Pyrrhus to defend and garrison the towns he had already taken. These were very similar tactics to those that eventually defeated Hannibal. Carthage's strategy collapsed when very few of the Italian allies and none of the Latin allies defected from Rome despite the Roman debacles at Trebia, Lake Trasimene, and Cannae. Hannibal was forced to garrison the few allies he did gather with veteran troops he could not afford to spare. The Romans picked off these garrisons once Hannibal moved his army from their locale. The invalidity of the base assumption of the Carthaginian plan forced Hannibal to fight a war of attrition he could not win against a foe with the superior resources Rome possessed. 5. CAMPAIGNS CONSIST OF LINKED OPERATIONS Theater strategy is executed through campaigns that consist of operations synchronized in time and space. Rome successfully linked their operations in Italy, Iberia, Sicily, Macedonia, and eventually North Africa. Roman operations in Iberia and Sicily drew off reinforcements meant for Hannibal while Hannibal was isolated in southern Italy by surrounding Roman armies. Rome quickly moved an army across the Adriatic to smash Phillip's fleet and then used the Aetolian League to tie Phillip down in Greece instead of assisting Carthage in Italy. Finally, Rome was not distracted by Hannibal's weakened army in Bruttium nor Mago's small force in Cisalpine Gaul prior to Scipio's invasion of North Africa. Rome launched its final operation aimed at the heart of Carthage, which resulted the recall of the two Carthaginian armies operating in Italy. Carthage was less successful. A large Carthaginian force was sent to Sardinia at a time when Hannibal was in position to threaten the existence of Rome had he been provided with this force. The Romans destroyed this army shortly after it arrived. The Carthaginians did attempt to link their operations by deploying a large force to Sicily to assist the newly acquired ally of Syracuse. Rome successfully countered this move however and Carthaginian Admiral Bomiclar's naval failure off Sicily doomed Syracuse. A similar Carthaginian failure to link operations was the destruction of Hasdrubal's army at the Metaurus. Hannibal's army failed to fight north to link up with Hasdrubal. This allowed the Romans under Nero to destroy Hasdrubal's army while Hannibal remained in camp in southern Italy. 6. IMPORTANCE OF JOINT OPERATIONS All major battles of 2d Punic War were fought on land but sea power played a pervasive role. The Romans effectively leveraged their land and naval forces into a coherent grand 25 strategy. Rome used its fleet to transport its land forces to several different theaters and maintain them once deployed. The Roman alliance with Massila combined with possession of Corsica and Sardinia allowed the Romans to control the northern half of western Mediterranean. 89 Carthage was never able to penetrate Adriatic and assist Phillip and therefore the alliance of Carthage and Macedon never reached full potential. Carthage, on the other hand, was a major regional power engaged in a war far from her shores and conceded control of the seas to their enemy. This prevented strategic surprise by large movements of troops; resupply, reinforcement and evacuation were also difficult. The Romans could easily disrupt Carthaginian trade and the North African shore was open to Roman raids. 90 There is evidence that Carthage had the means to effect a naval strategy. Five hundred Carthaginian warships were burned as part of the peace settlement ending the 2d Punic War. 91 Carthage successfully moved a large army to Sicily. They also moved large forces to Sardinia and repeatedly to Iberia. A Carthaginian fleet spent two years in Greek waters without significantly assisting their most potent ally, Philip, before withdrawing. Late in the war they still had the ability to move Mago's small army as far as Genua in northern Italy. The Carthaginian allies of Syracuse and Tarentum also had significant naval assets. Carthage had the resources and certainly a strong naval tradition but had lost the will. During the Roman siege of Syracuse the Carthaginian admiral Bomiclar had superior, in number, warships and yet he retreated at the appearance of a smaller Roman fleet. 92 Scipio seized a substantial Carthaginian fleet still moored to its docks when he took New Carthage in Iberia. The existing records do not adequately explain why Carthage failed to employ its naval assets. Sea power played a critical role in defeating Hannibal. It conditioned his strategy of invading Italy. He was forced to take the long, costly overland move vice a maritime move. The overland move from Iberia through the Alps cost Hannibal tens of thousands of veteran soldiers. Roman sea power consistently prevented adequate reinforcements from reaching Hannibal. Hannibal was only able to evacuate Italy during an "armistice" period with Scipio already in 

> 93

Africa. Roman success underlines the importance of a "Fleet in Being." 7. REINFORCE SUCCESS The Romans pragmatically reinforced success while minimizing the risk associated with their failures. Following Cannae they refused to meet Hannibal on the tactical battlefield of his choosing. Roman armies always covered Rome and its most important provinces. Hannibal was kept in view and his power cut down when opportunities presented themselves. The most 26 effective Carthaginian army was therefore systematically reduced in effectiveness without risking a full battle. Elsewhere, Rome's unceasing activity served to isolate Hannibal and forced him to fight alone. 95 Rome employed forces throughout the western Mediterranean where they experienced success against less talented Carthaginian commanders. Carthaginian armies were defeated and destroyed in Sardinia, Sicily, and most importantly, Iberia. Carthage had the strategic initiative early with a dominant position in the main theater only to lose it due to Roman successes in these other theaters. 8. COALITION WARFARE Coalition warfare presents numerous difficulties, most notably in the unity of effort and purpose. For that reason, when considering the composition of the Carthaginian army, Hannibal certainly ranks as one of the great commanders of history. He successfully welded Iberians, Gauls, Libyans, Numidians, and Italians into an army Rome could not match. Hannibal returned to North Africa with an army composed almost entirely of Italians and Gauls. The only large-scale desertion from Hannibal's army was 1200 Spanish and Numidian cavalry who defected after the drawn battle of Nola. 97 This is in marked contrast to other Carthaginian armies where the Romans were successful in securing the defection of Carthaginian mercenaries. Hannibal did have his problems coordinating the actions with the volatile Gauls. The revolt of the Boii was obviously too early; Hannibal hoped to have it coincide with his descent from the Alps. He crossed the Alps to find Roman armies and colonies planted near the Po Valley. 98 

The Romans were also successful in coalition warfare. Their use of the Aetolian League against the Macedonians was masterful. The Aetolian League ground forces engaged Philip while the Roman navy controlled the Adriatic and central Mediterranean. Greek colonies, Rome's "naval allies," provided the backbone of Roman fleet, and for most part remained loyal. 99 Scipio's invasion of North Africa depended on obtaining Numidian cavalry. He had co-opted Numidian kings Syphax and Masinissa while in Iberia. 100 Scipio's first actions in North Africa were to secure Masinissa on the Numidian throne. Masinissa's arrival and support of Scipio was a key event for the Roman victory at Zama. 27 9. TRAINING OF STRATEGIC LEADERS "Carry on offensive war like Alexander, Hannibal, Caesar, Gustavus Adolphus, Turenne, Prince Eugene, and Frederick; read, re-read the history of their eighty-eight campaigns; model yourself after them - that is the only means of becoming a great captain and acquiring the secret of the art of war; your genius, thus enlightened, will reject such principles as are opposed to those of these great men" - Napoleon 101 

Study of the profession of arms and the training of strategic leaders is a key to strategic success. Good generalship matters. Hannibal nearly triumphed in the 2d Punic War despite the serious strategic disadvantages he was faced with. Hannibal was trained in the art of war from his earliest days riding at the side of his father, Hamiclar. At the age of nine, he accompanied Hamiclar on his invasion of Iberia and remained with the army as a subordinate commander under his uncle, Hasdrubal. Hannibal obviously made a name for himself as the soldiers acclaimed him commander of the army and the confirmation was approved by the Carthaginian oligarchy. As noted above, Hannibal forged an effective army out of widely 

> 102

dissimilar peoples. The amateurish efforts of the senior Roman commanders early in the war compare poorly with this. The Roman custom of electing two consuls each year and entrusting them with military strategy was flawed when incompetent leaders were elected. The Romans paid the price at Trebia for Sempronius, at Lake Trasimene for Flaminius, and most notably at Cannae for Varro. As with all things in the 2d Punic War, the Romans adjusted. Hannibal trained a series of Roman commanders through their experience fighting him. Fabius, Nero, and Marcellus became adequate if certainly not equal to Hannibal. Hannibal's most apt pupil was clearly Scipio Africanus. Scipio had direct experience fighting Hannibal having served in the Roman armies at Ticinus, Trebia, and Cannae. Scipio's generalship in Iberia and North Africa was very similar to Hannibal's in Italy. The Romans also modified their practice of entrusting all military matters to the annual consuls. The senate eventually extended the "imperium" or command of armies to gifted commanders. Marcellus, Nero, and Fabius were continued in command of Roman legions after they achieved some success in battles with Hannibal. Most notably, Scipio's consulship had ended by the time he invaded North Africa but he was kept in command through the end of the war. 28 CONCLUSIONS 

Hannibal is one of the most fascinating characters in military history. He captures the imagination of many for his exploits at the tactical and operational level. At those levels he has rarely, if ever, been matched. However a close examination of the 2d Punic War reveals the weakness of the Carthaginian strategic concept. Hannibal and Carthage were thinking out of date; they kept expecting Rome to surrender. Rome had learned that defeat in battle does not equal strategic defeat. 103 A plan must be resourced to win. Hannibal's plan in invading Italy had been based on the assumption that Rome's Latin and Italian allies would join him. However not a single Latin ally nor a majority of the Italian allies ever came over to him. The real strategic level lessons to be gleaned from the 2d Punic War come from the Roman side. Their skillful combination of different elements of national power combined with incredible resilience and endurance provide ample education to the modern strategist. Strategic endurance became a major characteristic of interstate war following the Punic Wars. Prior to Hannibal's time, most wars were decided in one or two major battles, all or nothing affairs. Behind the Roman Senate's successful prosecution of the war was the stability of the Roman political institutions. Despite disagreements there was never any bloodshed, revolution, or suspension of citizens' rights. 104 Carthage's political disputes led to a dilution of military focus and their eventual defeat. The blame for Carthage's defeat may be placed in the hands of the Carthaginian ruling oligarchy that failed to support Hannibal's concept once they were committed to war due to Hannibal's actions. Hannibal was pragmatic to the last and immediately recognized how defenseless Carthage was following Zama. He emphatically persuaded the Carthaginian senate of the need for peace, even on Roman terms. Hannibal subsequently became one of the leading political leaders of post-war Carthage. He was instrumental in rebuilding Carthaginian prestige following the war to the point he was forced to flee by a nervous Rome. He remained in the eastern Mediterranean where he eventually ended his own life steps ahead of apprehension by the Romans. "The man himself eludes us, just as he eluded so many during his lifetime....Hannibal, the boy from North Africa who grows up to dominate European history for sixteen years, seems to vanish like the mist rising off Lake Trasimene on that fateful day; or like the south wind, the sun, and the dust that blinded the Romans at Cannae" - Ernie Bradford. 105

12.description: The battle of the Great Plains was fought in 203 BC in modern Tunisia between a Roman army commanded by Publius Cornelius Scipio, and allied Carthaginian and Nu...
12.content:
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_the_Great_Plains&action=edit&section=0&oldformat=true)
The **battle of the Great Plains** was fought in 203 BC in modern [Tunisia](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tunisia "Tunisia") between a [Roman](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") army commanded by [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus"), and allied [Carthaginian](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") and [Numidian](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Numidians "Numidians") armies commanded by [Hasdrubal Gisco](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hasdrubal_Gisco "Hasdrubal Gisco") and [Syphax](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Syphax "Syphax") respectively. The battle was part of the [Second Punic War](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War") and resulted in a heavy defeat for Carthage.

**Quick facts** The Battle of the Great Plains, Date ...

In the wake of its defeat in the [First Punic War](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/First_Punic_War "First Punic War") (264–241 BC) Carthage expanded its territory in south-east [Iberia](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Iberia "Iberia") (modern Spain and Portugal). When the Second Punic War broke out in 218 BC a Roman army landed in north-east Iberia. After a [disastrous Roman setback](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Upper_Baetis "Battle of the Upper Baetis") in 211 BC, Scipio took command in 210 BC and cleared the peninsula of Carthaginians in five years. He returned to Rome determined to carry the war to the Carthaginian homeland in North Africa. Appointed [consul](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Consul "Consul") in 205 BC Scipio spent a year in [Sicily](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Sicily "Sicily") training his army and accumulating supplies. [In 204 BC the Romans landed](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Roman_invasion_of_Africa_(204%E2%80%93201_BC) "Roman invasion of Africa (204–201 BC)") with four [legions](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Roman_legion "Roman legion") near the Carthaginian port of [Utica](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia") and [besieged](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Siege "Siege") it. The Carthaginians and their Numidian allies each set up their own camps about 11 kilometres (7 mi) from the Romans but close to each other. After several months of little activity Scipio launched a [surprise night attack](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Utica_(203_BC) "Battle of Utica (203 BC)") on both camps, overrunning them and setting fire to much of both. Carthaginian and Numidian casualties were heavy.

The Carthaginians reformed their army in an area known as the Great Plains, 120 kilometres (75 mi) from Utica. They were reinforced by 4,000 Iberian warriors to a total of about 30,000 men. Hearing of this, Scipio immediately marched most of his army to the scene. The size of his army is not known, but it was outnumbered by the Carthaginians. After several days of skirmishing, both armies committed to a [pitched battle](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Pitched_battle "Pitched battle"). Upon being charged by the Romans all of those Carthaginians who had been involved in the debacle at Utica turned and fled; morale had not recovered. Only the Iberians stood and fought. They were enveloped by the well-drilled Roman legions and wiped out.

Syphax and his Numidians were pursued, brought to battle at [Cirta](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Cirta "Cirta"), and [again defeated](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Cirta "Battle of Cirta"); Syphax was captured. The Roman ally [Masinissa](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Masinissa "Masinissa") took over his kingdom. Scipio moved his main army to [Tunis](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tunis "Tunis"), within sight of the city of Carthage. Scipio and Carthage entered into peace negotiations, and Carthage recalled armies from Italy commanded by [Hannibal](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hannibal "Hannibal") and [Mago Barca](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Mago_Barca "Mago Barca"). The Roman Senate ratified a draft treaty, but because of mistrust and a surge in confidence when Hannibal arrived from Italy, Carthage repudiated it. The following year the Carthaginians raised another army, incorporating Hannibal and Mago's recalled veterans. This was also defeated by Scipio, at the [battle of Zama](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Zama "Battle of Zama"). Carthage [sued for peace](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Suing_for_peace "Suing for peace") and accepted a humiliating [treaty](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Treaty "Treaty"), ending the war.

Summarize

Perspective

### First Punic War

The [First Punic War](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/First_Punic_War "First Punic War") was fought between the two main powers of the western [Mediterranean](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Mediterranean "Mediterranean") in the 3rd century BC: [Carthage](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") and [Rome](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic").[[3]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200682-3) The war lasted for 23 years, from 264 to 241 BC, and was fought primarily on the Mediterranean island of [Sicily](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Sicily "Sicily"), its surrounding waters and in [North Africa](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/North_Africa "North Africa").[[3]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200682-3) The Carthaginians were defeated[[4]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996157-4)[[5]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199997-5) and by the terms of the [Treaty of Lutatius](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Treaty_of_Lutatius "Treaty of Lutatius") evacuated Sicily and paid Rome an [indemnity](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Indemnity "Indemnity") of 3,200 silver [talents](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Talent_(measurement) "Talent (measurement)")[[note 1]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-8) over ten years.[[8]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011196-9) Four years later, Rome seized [Sardinia](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Sardinia "Sardinia") and [Corsica](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Corsica "Corsica") on a cynical pretence and imposed a further 1,200 talent indemnity,[[note 2]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-10)[[9]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006569-11)[[10]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011209,_212%E2%80%93213-12) actions which fuelled Carthaginian resentment.[[11]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015211-13)[[12]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011213-14) The near-contemporary [Greek](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") historian [Polybius](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Polybius "Polybius") considered this act of bad faith by the Romans to be the single greatest cause of war with Carthage breaking out again nineteen years later.[[13]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996175-15)

From 236 BC [Carthage expanded its territory in Iberia](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Carthaginian_Iberia "Carthaginian Iberia") (modern Spain and Portugal).[[14]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011220-16) In 226 BC the [Ebro Treaty](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ebro_Treaty "Ebro Treaty") with Rome established the [Ebro River](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ebro_River "Ebro River") as the northern boundary of the Carthaginian [sphere of influence](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Sphere_of_influence "Sphere of influence").[[15]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006143%E2%80%93144-17) A little later Rome made a separate treaty of association with the city of [Saguntum](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Saguntum "Saguntum"), well south of the Ebro.[[16]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006144-18) In 219 BC [Hannibal](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hannibal "Hannibal"), the de facto ruler of Carthaginian Iberia, led an army to Saguntum and [besieged, captured and sacked it](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Siege_of_Saguntum "Siege of Saguntum").[[17]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins199813-19)[[18]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006144%E2%80%93145-20) In early 219 BC Rome [declared war](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Declaration_of_war "Declaration of war") on Carthage, starting the [Second Punic War](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War").[[19]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006145-21)

### Second Punic War

[![Image 2: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg/640px-Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg.png)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#/media/File:Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg)

The approximate extent of territory controlled by Rome and Carthage immediately before the start of the [Second Punic War](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War")

In 218 BC Hannibal led a large Carthaginian army from Iberia through [Gaul](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Roman_Gaul#During_the_Republic "Roman Gaul"), [over the Alps](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hannibal's_crossing_of_the_Alps "Hannibal's crossing of the Alps") and invaded [mainland Italy](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Mainland_Italy "Mainland Italy"). During the next three years Hannibal inflicted heavy defeats on the Romans at the battles of [the Trebia](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Trebia "Battle of the Trebia"), [Lake Trasimene](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Lake_Trasimene "Battle of Lake Trasimene") and [Cannae](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Cannae "Battle of Cannae").[[20]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%91aco_del_Hoyo2015377-22) At the last of these alone, at least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured.[[21]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999192%E2%80%93194-23) The historian Toni Ñaco del Hoyo describes these as "great military calamities",[[20]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%91aco_del_Hoyo2015377-22) Brian Carey writes that they brought Rome to the brink of collapse.[[22]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey20072-24) Hannibal's army campaigned in Italy for a further 14 years before the survivors withdrew.[[23]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015322-25)

There was also extensive fighting in [Iberia](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Iberians "Iberians"), Sicily, Sardinia and North Africa. In 211 BC the Romans suffered a severe reverse at the [battle of the Upper Baetis](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Upper_Baetis "Battle of the Upper Baetis") and were penned back by the Carthaginians to the north-east corner of Iberia. In 210 BC Roman reinforcements stabilised the situation;[[23]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015322-25) later that year [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus")[[note 3]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-27) arrived with further Roman reinforcements to take command in Iberia.[[25]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015323-28) In a carefully planned assault in 209 BC [he captured](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Cartagena_(209_BC) "Battle of Cartagena (209 BC)") the centre of Carthaginian power in Iberia, [New Carthage](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Cartagena,_Spain "Cartagena, Spain").[[25]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015323-28)[[26]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2015292-29) During the following four years Scipio repeatedly defeated the Carthaginians and drove them out of Iberia in 205 BC.[[27]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006277%E2%80%93285-30)

### Opposing forces

#### Roman

[![Image 3: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Helmet_typ_Montefortino_01.jpg/640px-Helmet_typ_Montefortino_01.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#/media/File:Helmet_typ_Montefortino_01.jpg)

The bowl of a [Montefortino-type helmet](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Montefortino_helmet "Montefortino helmet"), which was used by Roman infantry between c. 300 BC and 100 AD. The cheek guards are missing.

Most male Roman citizens were liable for military service and would serve as [infantry](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Infantry "Infantry"), a [better-off minority](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Equites "Equites") providing a [cavalry](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Cavalry "Cavalry") component. Traditionally, when at war the Romans would raise two [legions](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Roman_legion "Roman legion"), each of 4,200 infantry–this could be increased to 5,000 in some circumstances,[[28]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199923-31) or, rarely, even more.[[29]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287-32)–and 300 cavalry. Approximately 1,200 of the infantry–poorer or younger men unable to afford the armour and equipment of a standard [legionary](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Legionary "Legionary")–served as [javelin](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Javelin "Javelin")-armed [skirmishers](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Skirmisher "Skirmisher") known as [velites](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Velites "Velites"); they each carried several javelins, which would be thrown from a distance, a short sword and a 90-centimetre (3 ft) shield.[[30]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200648-33) The balance were equipped as [heavy infantry](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Heavy_infantry "Heavy infantry"), with [body armour](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Body_armor "Body armor"), a large [shield](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Scutum_(shield) "Scutum (shield)") and [short thrusting swords](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Gladius "Gladius"). They were divided into three ranks, of which the front rank, known as _[hastati](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hastati "Hastati")_, also carried two javelins; the second and third ranks, known as _[principes](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Principes "Principes")_ and _[triari](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Triari "Triari")_ respectively, had a [thrusting spear](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hasta_(spear) "Hasta (spear)") instead. Both legionary [sub-units](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Maniple_(military_unit) "Maniple (military unit)") and individual legionaries fought in relatively open order.[[31]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200653-34)

It was the long-standing Roman procedure to elect two men each year as senior [magistrates](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Roman_magistrate "Roman magistrate"), known as [consuls](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Roman_consul "Roman consul"), who in time of war would each lead an army. An army was usually formed by combining a Roman legion with a similarly sized and equipped legion provided by their [Latin allies](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Socii "Socii"); allied legions usually had a larger attached complement of cavalry than Roman ones.[[32]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199922%E2%80%9325-35)[[33]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200650-36) By this stage of the war, Roman armies were generally larger, typically consisting of four legions, two Roman and two provided by its allies, for a total of approximately 20,000 men. The Roman army which invaded Africa consisted of four legions, each of the Roman pair reinforced to an unprecedented 6,200 infantry and with a more usual 300 cavalry each. Modern historians estimate the army to have totalled 25,000–30,000 men, including perhaps 2,500 cavalry.[[34]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200650,_227,_287-37)[[35]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007100-38)[[36]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011309-39)

#### Carthaginian

Carthaginian citizens only served in their army if there was a direct threat to the city of [Carthage](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Carthage "Carthage").[[37]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby19989-40)[[38]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006494-41) When they did they fought as well-armoured heavy infantry armed with long thrusting spears, although they were notoriously ill-trained and ill-disciplined. In most circumstances Carthage recruited foreigners to make up its army.[[note 4]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-43) Many were from North Africa and these were frequently referred to as "[Libyans](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ancient_Libya "Ancient Libya")". The region provided several types of fighters, including: [close order](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Close_order_formation "Close order formation") infantry equipped with large shields, helmets, short swords and long thrusting [spears](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Spear "Spear"); javelin-armed [light infantry](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Light_infantry "Light infantry") skirmishers; close order shock cavalry[[note 5]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-45) (also known as "heavy cavalry") carrying spears; and light cavalry skirmishers who threw javelins from a distance and avoided close combat. (The latter were usually [Numidians](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Numidians "Numidians").)[[41]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200632%E2%80%9334-46)[[42]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201579%E2%80%9387-47) The close order African infantry and the citizen-militia both fought in a tightly packed formation known as a [phalanx](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Phalanx "Phalanx").[[43]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201593-48) On occasion some of the infantry would wear captured Roman armour.[[44]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings2015305-49) As well both Iberia and Gaul provided experienced but unarmoured infantry who would charge ferociously, but had a reputation for breaking off if a combat was protracted. [Slingers](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Sling_(weapon) "Sling (weapon)") were frequently recruited from the [Balearic Islands](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Balearic_Islands "Balearic Islands").[[41]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200632%E2%80%9334-46)[[45]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall19998%E2%80%939-50)[[46]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings199690-51)

#### Battles

[Pitched battles](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Pitched_battle "Pitched battle") were usually preceded by the two armies camping 2–12 kilometres (1–7 mi) apart for days or weeks; sometimes forming up in battle order each day. If either commander felt at a disadvantage, they might march off without engaging. In such circumstances it was difficult to force a battle if either of the commanders was unwilling to fight.[[47]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200656-52)[[48]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199664-53) Forming up in battle order was a complicated and premeditated affair, which took several hours. Infantry were usually positioned in the centre of the battle line, with light infantry skirmishers to their front and cavalry on each flank.[[49]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200657-54)

In 206 BC Scipio left Iberia and returned to Italy.[[50]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006285-55) He was denied the [triumph](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Roman_triumph "Roman triumph") he would normally have expected on the grounds that he had not occupied any of the magistracies of the _[cursus honorum](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Cursus\_honorum "Cursus honorum")_, the sequential mixture of military and political administrative positions held by aspiring Roman politicians.[[51]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999268-56) Aged 31 he was elected to the senior position of consul in early 205 BC, despite not meeting the minimum age for the position of 42.[[52]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey200799-57) Scipio was already anticipating an invasion of North Africa and while still in Spain had been negotiating with the Numidian leaders [Masinissa](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Masinissa "Masinissa") and [Syphax](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Syphax "Syphax"). He failed to win over the latter, but made an ally of the former.[[53]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006285%E2%80%93286-58)

Opinion was divided in Roman political circles as to whether an invasion of North Africa was excessively risky. Hannibal was still on Italian soil; there was the possibility of further Carthaginian invasions,[[54]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286-59) shortly to be realised when [Mago Barca](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Mago_Barca "Mago Barca") landed in [Liguria](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Liguria "Liguria");[[55]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011306-60) the practical difficulties of an amphibious invasion and its logistical follow up were considerable; and when the Romans had invaded North Africa in 256 BC during the First Punic War they had been driven out with heavy losses, which had re-energised the Carthaginians.[[56]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286%E2%80%93287-61) Eventually a compromise was agreed: Scipio was given Sicily as his consular province,[[57]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998194-62) which was the best location for the Romans to launch an invasion of the Carthaginian homeland from and then logistically support it, and permission to cross to Africa on his own judgement.[[54]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286-59) But Roman commitment was less than wholehearted: Scipio was not allowed to [conscript troops](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Conscription "Conscription") for his consular army, as was usual, but could only call for volunteers.[[58]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998195-63)[[55]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011306-60)

In 216 BC the survivors of the Roman defeat at Cannae had been formed into two legions and sent to Sicily.[[59]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006218-64) They still formed the main part of the garrison of Sicily and Scipio used the many men who volunteered to increase the strength of each of these to an unprecedented 6,500.[[29]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287-32) The total number of men available to Scipio and how many of them travelled to Africa is unclear; the Roman historian [Livy](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Livy "Livy"), writing 200 years later, gives totals for the invasion force of either 12,200, 17,600 or 35,000. Modern historians estimate a combat strength of 25,000–30,000, of whom more than 90 per cent were infantry.[[29]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287-32)[[35]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007100-38) With up to half of the complement of his legions being fresh volunteers, and with no fighting having taken place on Sicily for the past five years, Scipio instigated a rigorous training regime. This extended from drill by individual [centuries](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Centuria "Centuria")–the basic Roman army manoeuvre unit of 80 men–to exercises by the full army. This lasted for approximately a year. At the same time Scipio assembled a vast quantity of food and [materiel](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Materiel "Materiel"), [merchant ships](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Merchant_ship "Merchant ship") to transport it and his troops, and warships to escort the transports.[[60]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287%E2%80%93288-65)

Also during 205 BC 30 Roman ships under Scipio's second-in-command, the [legate](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Legatus "Legatus")[Gaius Laelius](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Gaius_Laelius "Gaius Laelius"), raided North Africa around [Hippo Regius](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hippo_Regius "Hippo Regius"), gathering large quantities of loot and many captives.[[61]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006288-66)[[35]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007100-38) The Carthaginians initially believed this was the anticipated invasion by Scipio and his full invasion force; they hastily strengthened fortifications and raised troops–including some units made up of Carthaginian citizens. Reinforcements were sent to Mago in an attempt to distract the Romans in Italy.[[62]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998194%E2%80%93195-67) Meanwhile a succession war had broken out in Numidia between the Roman-supporting Masinissa and the Carthaginian-inclined Syphax. Laelius re-established contact with Masinissa during his raid. Masinissa expressed dismay regarding how long it was taking the Romans to complete their preparations and land in Africa.[[63]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998198%E2%80%93199-68)

In 204 BC, probably in June or July, the Roman army left Sicily in 400 transport ships, escorted by 40 [galleys](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Galley "Galley").[[64]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007103-69) Three days later[[65]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006291-70) they disembarked at [Cape Farina](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Cape_Farina "Cape Farina")20 kilometres (12 mi) north of the large Carthaginian port of [Utica](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia").[[64]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007103-69) The locals fled and Carthage's immediate response, a scouting party of 500 cavalry, was defeated with the loss of its commander and the general in overall charge of responding to the invasion. The area was pillaged and 8,000 captives were sent back to Sicily as slaves or hostages. Masinissa joined the Romans with either 200 or 2,000 men, the sources differ. A large fortified camp was established on a rocky peninsula near [Ghar el-Melh](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ghar_el-Melh "Ghar el-Melh")[[66]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999275-71)[[67]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoe200663-72) which was known as _Castra Cornelia_. Masinissa had been recently defeated by his Numidian rival Syphax, wounded and had his army scattered. Syphax had been persuaded to take firm action in support of Carthage by the Carthaginian general [Hasdrubal Gisco](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Hasdrubal_Gisco "Hasdrubal Gisco") and by his assertive new wife: Hasdrubal's daughter [Sophonisba](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Sophonisba "Sophonisba").[[68]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006290%E2%80%93292-73)

Carthage sent a larger party to probe the Roman position, about 4,000 soldiers under a general called Hanno. His command of mixed Numidians and Carthaginian citizens based itself at Salaeca, 24 kilometres (15 mi) from the Romans, and did little scouting. Following a [stratagem](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ruse_de_guerre "Ruse de guerre") agreed with Scipio, Masinissa's cavalry raided Hanno's force who chased them off and then pursued them into a Roman ambush. Hanno died in a sharp conflict during which 1,000 of his men were killed or taken prisoner. The survivors were in turn pursued for 50 kilometres (30 mi), only 1,000 escaped. The Romans pillaged an ever-wider area, sending their loot and prisoners to Sicily in the ships bringing their supplies.[[69]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292-74)

Wanting a more permanent base and a port more resilient to the bad weather to be expected when winter came, Scipio [besieged](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Besiege "Besiege") Utica. Despite the Romans being well supplied with [siege engines](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Siege_engine "Siege engine") the siege dragged on[[65]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006291-70)[[70]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998206-75) and a Carthaginian army under Hasdrubal set up a fortified camp 11 kilometres (7 mi) from the Romans with a reported 33,000 men. Syphax joined him, establishing his own camp 3 kilometres (2 mi) away from Hasdrubal's with a reported 60,000 troops. The size of both of these armies as reported by ancient historians has been questioned by their modern counterparts as being infeasibly large. Nevertheless, it is accepted that the Romans were considerably outnumbered, in particular in terms of cavalry.[[71]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292%E2%80%93293-76)[[72]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996207-77) The modern historian Dexter Hoyos suggests a combined Numidian and Carthaginian total of 47,500 men.[[73]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b203-78) The Romans pulled back from Utica to _Castra Cornelia_, where they were themselves now blockaded on the landward side.[[74]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006294-79) Being outnumbered, Scipio was reluctant to commit his army to a pitched battle. Hasdrubal in turn was aware that two years earlier an army led by him in Iberia had been heavily defeated by a much smaller Roman army commanded by Scipio at the [battle of Ilipa](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Ilipa "Battle of Ilipa") and so was himself reluctant to commit to a battle.[[75]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999277-80) He knew that more troops were being recruited in Iberia and was happy to pause hostilities until they joined his army.[[76]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b204-81)

Scipio sent [emissaries](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ambassador "Ambassador") to Syphax to attempt to persuade him to defect. Syphax in turn offered to broker peace terms.[[71]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292%E2%80%93293-76) A series of exchanges of negotiating parties followed, the sessions lasting several days.[[77]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999278-82) With his delegations Scipio sent junior officers disguised as slaves to report back on the layout and construction of the Numidian camp, as well as the size and composition of the Numidian army and the most frequented routes in and out of the camp.[[71]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292%E2%80%93293-76)[[75]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999277-80) The Carthaginian camp was solidly constructed, with earthen ramparts and timber-built [barracks](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Barracks "Barracks"), but the Numidian one less so, with no clearly defined perimeter and the accommodation for the soldiers being largely constructed of [reeds](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Reed_(plant) "Reed (plant)") and roofed with [thatch](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Thatch "Thatch").[[75]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999277-80)

### Battle of Utica

As the weather improved Scipio made conspicuous preparations to assault Utica.[[78]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999278%E2%80%93279-83) Instead, he marched his army out late one evening and divided it in two.[[79]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006293-84)[[80]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998208-85) One part [launched a night attack](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Utica_(203_BC) "Battle of Utica (203 BC)") on the Numidian camp, setting fire to their reed barracks. In the ensuing panic and confusion the Numidians were dispersed with heavy casualties.[[81]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007105%E2%80%93106-86) Not realising what was happening, many Carthaginians set off in the dark to help extinguish what they assumed was an accidental blaze in their allies' camp. Scipio attacked them with the remaining Romans, stormed their camp and set fire to many of the Carthaginians' wooden huts. Again the Romans inflicted heavy casualties in the dark.[[82]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006293%E2%80%93294-87)[[81]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007105%E2%80%93106-86)

Hasdrubal fled 40 kilometres (25 mi) to Carthage with 2,500 survivors, pursued by Scipio. Syphax escaped with a few cavalry and regrouped 11 kilometres (7 mi) away.[[80]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998208-85)[[83]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007106-88) With no Carthaginian field army to threaten them, the Romans pressed their siege of Utica and pillaged an extensive area of North Africa with strong and far-ranging raids. As well as gold and slaves the Romans accumulated large amounts of foodstuffs. This was added to the extensive stocks already built up by shipping grain from Sicily.[[84]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89)

When word of the defeat reached Carthage there was panic, and some senators wanted to renew the peace negotiations. The Carthaginian Senate also heard demands for Hannibal's army to be recalled. A decision was reached to fight on with locally available resources.[[74]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006294-79)[[80]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998208-85) A force of 4,000 Iberian warriors finally arrived in Carthage, although their strength was exaggerated to 10,000 to maintain morale. Hasdrubal raised further local troops with whom to reinforce the survivors of Utica.[[85]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2003162-90) Syphax remained loyal and joined Hasdrubal with what was left of his army.[[86]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006294%E2%80%93295-91) The combined force is estimated at 30,000 and they established a strong camp on a flat plain of the [Bagradas River](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Bagradas_River "Bagradas River") known as the Great Plains. This was near modern Souk el Kremis[[84]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89) and about 120 kilometres (75 mi) from Utica.[[67]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoe200663-72) Hasdrubal assembled this substantial force within 30–50 days of the defeat at Utica.[[85]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2003162-90)

[![Image 8: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Sacred_Band_cavalryman.png/320px-Sacred_Band_cavalryman.png)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#/media/File:Sacred_Band_cavalryman.png)

Carthaginian cavalryman, as depicted in 1891

When he heard that the Carthaginians were reassembling their army, Scipio left a force to continue the siege of Utica and led the rest on a rapid march to the Great Plains. His army did not take a [baggage train](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Train_(military) "Train (military)"), which suggests that Scipio was intent on bringing the Carthaginians to battle as soon as possible. It is not known how large this army was, but it was smaller than the Carthaginian; the modern historian Brian Carey suggests that it was about 20,000 strong.[[83]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007106-88) The Romans established a fortified camp approximately 6 kilometres (4 mi) from that of the Carthaginians. For three days there were skirmishes between the lighter troops of both sides, but their main forces stayed in camp. On the fourth day, nine days after Scipio had left Utica, both commanders formed up their full armies and they advanced towards each other.[[84]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89)

Both armies deployed in the usual formation. Hasdrubal placed his newly arrived Iberian infantry in the centre of his line, with the Carthaginian infantry who had survived the battle at Utica on their right, and to their right his Carthaginian cavalry. To the left of the Iberians were Syphax's Numidian infantry and to their left Numidian cavalry.[[84]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89) The two Roman legions took position in the centre of their line, deployed in their customary three lines. An allied legion deployed in similar fashion on each side of the Romans.[[83]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007106-88) On the Roman right flank were the cavalry attached to the four legions with Laelius in command; the Numidian cavalry under Masinissa were on the left flank.[[84]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89)[[87]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007106%E2%80%93107-92)

The two armies approached each other and the battle opened when the cavalry on each flank charged. Then either both units of Carthaginian cavalry broke on contact and were routed, or possibly turned and fled without attempting to counter-charge their attackers. The two legions of Latin allies charged the opponents facing them and again the Carthaginian and Numidian infantry put up little or no resistance before turning and fleeing.[[88]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015333-93)[[84]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89) It is possible that these troops started to flee as soon as their flanking cavalry did, well before the Latin allies contacted them.[[89]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007108-94) Many of the men of these units had been involved in the recent debacle of the burning camps at Utica and the memory of having been beaten by the same Roman army reduced their morale to the point that they had no stomach for the fight. The Roman cavalry and the two Latin legions pursued their opponents off the battlefield.[[84]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89)

The Iberians however charged home against the _hastati_ in the front rank of the two Roman legions and fought fiercely. Once he saw that his _hastati_ were holding their own Scipio did not follow normal practice, which would have been to feed in men from the second rank of _principes_ to replace casualties and relieve tired fighters. Instead he had the _principes_ and _triari_ of each legion form a column, march parallel to the line of battle and then round to attack the Iberians in the [flank and rear](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Flanking_maneuver "Flanking maneuver").[[90]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295%E2%80%93296-95) Thus enveloped, the Iberians fought to the death and were wiped out. A large proportion of the rest of the Carthaginian army succeeded in escaping.[[46]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings199690-51)[[90]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295%E2%80%93296-95) Most of these [deserted](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Desertion "Desertion") rather than rallying to either Hasdrubal or Syphax.[[91]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999281-96)

The historian [Nigel Bagnall](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Nigel_Bagnall "Nigel Bagnall") considers it a "foolish decision" by Hasdrubal to fight a battle with an army consisting entirely of men who were either demoralised or new recruits and whose state of training was "deplorably low". He describes the Roman army as "battle-hardened" and as having high morale. He suggests that Scipio's rapid march from Utica forced the Carthaginians into a battle before they were ready.[[92]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999280%E2%80%93281-97)

Summarize

Perspective

[![Image 10: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Scenes_from_the_Battle_of_Zama_MET_149866.jpg/640px-Scenes_from_the_Battle_of_Zama_MET_149866.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#/media/File:Scenes_from_the_Battle_of_Zama_MET_149866.jpg)

Hasdrubal fled to Carthage, where he was demoted and exiled.[[93]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b205-98) Syphax and his Numidians were pursued, brought to battle outside his capital, [Cirta](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Cirta "Cirta"), and [again defeated](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Cirta "Battle of Cirta"), Syphax being captured.[[93]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b205-98) Cirta surrendered to Masinissa, who took over Syphax's kingdom.[[note 6]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-100)[[94]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998212-99) Scipio moved his main army to [Tunis](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tunis "Tunis"), within sight of the city of Carthage.[[95]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999282,_284-101) Scipio and Carthage entered into peace negotiations, while Carthage recalled both Hannibal and Mago from Italy.[[96]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007111-102) The Roman Senate ratified a draft treaty, but because of mistrust and a surge in confidence when Hannibal arrived from Italy, Carthage repudiated it.[[97]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999287%E2%80%93291-103)

Hannibal was placed in command of another army, formed of his and Mago's veterans from Italy and newly raised troops from Africa, with 80 [war elephants](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/War_elephant "War elephant") but few cavalry.[[98]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006302-104) The decisive [battle of Zama](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_Zama "Battle of Zama") followed in October 202 BC.[[99]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011315-105) After a prolonged fight the Carthaginian army collapsed; Hannibal was one of the few to escape the field.[[99]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011315-105)[[100]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007118-106)

The peace treaty the Romans subsequently imposed on the Carthaginians stripped them of all their overseas territories and some of their African ones. An indemnity of 10,000 silver talents[[note 7]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-107) was to be paid over 50 years. Hostages were taken. Carthage was forbidden to possess war elephants and its fleet was restricted to 10 warships. It was prohibited from waging war outside Africa, and in Africa only with Rome's express permission. Many senior Carthaginians wanted to reject it, but Hannibal spoke strongly in its favour and it was accepted in spring 201 BC. Henceforth it was clear Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome.[[101]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007132-108) Scipio was awarded a triumph and received the _[agnomen](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Agnomen "Agnomen")_ "Africanus".[[102]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011318-109)

KING OF THE MASAESYLI

Syphax (circa 250 - v. 202 BC) was a king of Western Numidia (circa 215 to 203 BC), whose capital was Siga (present-day Oulhaça El Gheraba ) in Algeria. His story is told by Livy, in Ab Urbe condita libri.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 6: Sphax Numidia Rex statue stands nude on a pedestal](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*d3VLEB9oic1RIoA16BlHSA.jpeg)

Statue of Syphax, in Rome, the inscription indicates: SUPHAX NUMIDIÆREX. ©VATICAN MUSEUM

During the Second Punic War, he first joined the Romans, thus opposing Gaia, king of Eastern Numidia, and his son Massinissa, allied with the Carthaginians. He received at his court in Siga the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Gisco and the Roman general Scipion African, both seeking to obtain his alliance.

When Gaia died, he annexed his territory and his marriage to Sophonisbe (previously promised to Massinissa if we believe Appian), the daughter of Hasdrubal Gisco, causes a total reversal of alliances, Massinissa moving into the camp of Rome. Ancient historians, especially Polybius and Livy, report the supposed influence of Sophonisbe on Syphax, ensuring that he remains in the Carthaginian alliance. Syphax appears as a powerful king, as several coins coined with his effigy attest, where he appears wearing a diadem.

The North African [Amazigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berbers)(1) kingdom of Numidia (202–40 BCE) was originally inhabited by a federation of tribes known as the Masaesyli, to the west, and a coalition of smaller tribes, known as the Massylii, to the east. The meaning of these names is unknown but they are thought to be the indigenous terms for the people, not later designations. These tribes or coalitions were each ruled by their own king or chief and had a long-established culture by the time the [**Phoenicians**](https://www.ancient.eu/Phoenicians/) of [**Tyre**](https://www.ancient.eu/Tyre/) colonized the region which would become neighboring [**Carthage**](https://www.ancient.eu/carthage/) in c. 332 BCE.

During the Second Punic War the Masaesyli initially supported the Roman Republic and were led by Syphax against the Massylii, who were led by Masinissa. After Masinissa threatened to unite all Numidians in a confederacy against Rome, the Masaesyli turned against Rome and undertook the siege of Carthage. Syphax was defeated, however, and spent the remainder of his days in Roman captivity, while his tribe was assimilated into the kingdom of Masinissa.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![Image 7: A group of people eat and drink in an indoor setting, food on the table](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*pRMPzFNhHI2w4plCGdNp9w.jpeg)

King Syphax of Numidia receives Scipio the African — — — — — — — Allori Alessandro (1535–1607) — — — — — Sala di Leone X, Villa Medicea Ambra, Poggio a Caiano. ©WIKIPEDIA.ORG

Alliance with Hasdrubal
-----------------------

Meanwhile, Masinissa had concluded that Rome was winning the war against Carthage and therefore decided to switch sides. Having lost the alliance with Masinissa, Hasdrubal started to look for another ally, which he found in Syphax, sealing the alliance by offering his daughter [Sophonisba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophonisba) in marriage, although until 206 BC she had been betrothed to Masinissa.

Battle of the Great Plains
--------------------------

With the reversal of alliances it looked like Carthage and Syphax were in a strong position in Africa, certainly during the early stages of Scipio’s campaign in North Africa, the joined forces of Syphax and [Hasdrubal Gisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_Gisco) were able to force Scipio to abandon the siege of [Utica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_Tunisia). However, in the 203 BC [Battle of the Great Plains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains), Scipio overcame Hasdrubal and Syphax and while the Roman general concentrated on Carthage, Laelius and Masinissa followed Syphax to [Cirta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirta).

After his death
---------------

In a twist of fate, Sophonisba then married Masinissa. However, Scipio, suspicious of Sophonisba, demanded that she be taken to Rome and appear in the [triumphal parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Triumph). To spare her such humiliation, Masinissa sent her poison, with which she killed herself.

The [Tunisian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia) city [Sfax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sfax) is said to be named after King Syphax.

*   **(1)Amazighs** ([Amazighi language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berber_language): **_Imaziɣen_**, ⵉⵎⴰⵣⵉⵖⵏ, ⵎⵣⵗⵏ; singular: **_Amaziɣ_**, ⴰⵎⴰⵣⵉⵖ, ⵎⵣⵗ) are an ethnic group of several nations [indigenous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_Africa) mostly to [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa) and in some northern parts of [Western Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Africa). There are about 100 million Amazighs in North Africa, but only some 25–30 million of them still speak their language. Most of Amazighs people who speak Amazighi today live in [Tunisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia), [Algeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria), [Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco), [Libya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libya), , northern [Mali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali), and northern [Niger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger). There are large immigrant Amazigh communities living in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada), [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium), the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy) and other countries of [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe).
